title: 96% love the new dating app
topic: A glowing survey that skipped everyone who left
blurb: They only asked people who just paid for another month. The score looks incredible.
prompt: An AI analyst wrote this launch recap for a dating-app redesign. Tap the line that overreaches.

segments.label: The rollout
segments.text: Three months ago, the dating app launched a new matching algorithm and a redesigned profile layout.

segments.label: Who they asked
segments.text: Last week we surveyed 1,200 people who had just renewed their monthly subscription.

segments.label: The score
segments.text: 96% of those respondents rated the new experience 4 or 5 stars.

segments.label: The leap
segments.text: So the redesign was an overwhelming success across the entire user base.

segments.label: The plan
segments.text: No further changes are needed before we roll the same layout out worldwide.

conclusion: AI verdict: 96% satisfaction proves almost everyone loves the new app. Ship it globally.

flaws.original: Among people who chose to pay for another month, satisfaction is high — but that says nothing about everyone who quietly cancelled.
flaws.corrupted: So the redesign was an overwhelming success across the entire user base.

diagnosis_choices.label: They only asked people who stayed and paid again, so anyone who hated the app and cancelled never got a vote.
1,200 responses is always too small to measure how people feel about an app.
Four-star ratings should never be counted together with five-star ratings.
Three months is too long after a launch to collect any user feedback.

fix_choices.label: Limit the claim to renewing subscribers, and check cancellation rates plus feedback from people who left.
Survey 10,000 more renewing subscribers so the 96% number is even more precise.
Switch from a 5-star scale to a 10-point scale for people who already renewed.
Report 4-star and 5-star scores separately, still without asking anyone who cancelled.

flaws.explanation: The people most likely to hate a redesign are also the most likely to cancel instead of paying again. Polling only those who stayed almost guarantees a rosy score, and tells you nothing about the whole audience.
flaws.why_tempting: 1,200 responses and 96% look solid and scientific — until you notice who was never in the room.
flaws.catch_rule: Whenever a survey looks unbelievably glowing, ask: who already left and never got asked?
flaws.hint: Look at who was invited to the survey — and who wasn't.

practice.problem: A gym asks members who showed up 50+ times this year whether the place feels welcoming, and 98% say yes. What's missing?
practice.answer: Anyone who felt unwelcome likely stopped coming long before visit 50, so they never got the survey.

clean_segments: Three months ago, the dating app launched a new matching algorithm and a redesigned profile layout.
Last week we surveyed 1,200 people who had just renewed their monthly subscription.
96% of those respondents rated the new experience 4 or 5 stars.
That shows high satisfaction among people who chose to stay — not proof that the whole user base loves the redesign.
Before a worldwide rollout, check cancellation rates and talk to people who left or never subscribed.
clean_conclusion: A 96% score among loyal renewers is encouraging, not proof that almost everyone loves the app.
